```{r}
#| label: original-study

# Pan & Rivers (2023), Experiment 3: N = 52 analysed (8 excluded for failing attention checks).
# Summary values computed from the authors' public OSF data (https://osf.io/htjqz/):
#   predictions: "KUPE Globally Differentiated Predictions Data.xlsx", sheet kupe3gpredsrfile
#   recall:      "KUPE Criterial Test Data.xlsx", sheet kupe3finaltest (proportions; pretested
#                items guessed correctly at pretest are already removed)
# Check: these reproduce the paper's Exp 3 statistics exactly: cycle x condition interaction
# on predictions F(1, 51) = 10.92, p = .0017, partial eta^2 = .18; recall advantage for
# pretested pairs t(51) = 6.67 (Cycle 1) and 5.99 (Cycle 2).
original_n <- 52

original_pred <- tibble(        # predictions, 0-16
  cycle     = c(1, 1, 2, 2),
  condition = c("read", "pretest", "read", "pretest"),
  mean      = c(6.5577, 5.8462, 6.9231, 7.6154),
  sd        = c(3.3631, 3.4035, 3.4004, 3.4022),
  n         = original_n
)
original_recall <- tibble(      # proportion recalled on the criterial test
  cycle     = c(1, 1, 2, 2),
  condition = c("read", "pretest", "read", "pretest"),
  mean      = c(0.5084, 0.6825, 0.5493, 0.7178),
  sd        = c(0.2207, 0.1970, 0.2501, 0.2030),
  n         = original_n
)

# Key contrast, per participant: (pretest - read prediction in Cycle 2) minus
# (pretest - read prediction in Cycle 1). Its one-sample t-test is the 2 x 2 interaction:
# F(1, N - 1) = t^2. Mean and SD of the contrast from the OSF data.
original_contrast <- list(N = 52, mean = 1.4038, sd = 3.0631)
```

## Guidance

One row per study for the key comparison: the original, your Phase 1 replication, and your
Phase 2 extension. The table fills itself in from the data as each phase is exported, using the
analysis code below (open "Show the analysis code"), which is shared by both phases so they are
analysed identically. Edit that code once, here, to match your design and preregistered
exclusion rule. On the scientific-extension track, the Phase 2 row reports the new comparison:

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE, guess_max = 100000)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  # A consent decline also sets the saver completion flag. Count only consented
  # sessions that reached debrief as completed experimental procedures.
  consented_ids <- trials |>
    filter(task == "consent", as.logical(consented) %in% TRUE) |>
    distinct(participant_id)
  debrief_ids <- trials |> filter(task == "debrief") |> distinct(participant_id)
  complete <- participants |>
    filter(as.logical(completed)) |>
    semi_join(consented_ids, by = "participant_id") |>
    semi_join(debrief_ids, by = "participant_id")

  # Exclusion rule (replace with the rule you preregister). As in the original: exclude anyone
  # who failed either Cycle 1 attention check (the two "my prediction was higher / lower / the
  # same as how well I actually performed" questions). Also exclude anyone missing one of the
  # four predictions, since the key test needs all four.
  checks <- trials |>
    filter(task == "attention_check") |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(checks_passed = sum(as.logical(passed) %in% TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  n_preds <- trials |>
    filter(task == "prediction") |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(n_pred = sum(!is.na(prediction)), .groups = "drop")
  checked <- complete |>
    select(participant_id) |>
    left_join(checks, by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(n_preds, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(checks_passed   = replace_na(checks_passed, 0),
           n_pred          = replace_na(n_pred, 0),
           passed_checks   = checks_passed == 2,
           has_predictions = n_pred == 4)
  keep <- complete |>
    semi_join(filter(checked, passed_checks, has_predictions), by = "participant_id")

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, checked = checked, keep = keep,
       has_error_log = file.exists(errors_path))
}

# Predictions of analysed participants: one row per participant x cycle x condition.
prediction_data <- function(d) {
  d$trials |>
    filter(task == "prediction", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    transmute(participant_id, cycle = as.integer(cycle), condition, value = as.numeric(prediction))
}

# Criterial-test recall of analysed participants, proportion correct (lenient scoring) per
# participant x cycle x condition. Pretested pairs guessed correctly at pretest are dropped,
# as in the original (following Huelser & Metcalfe, 2012).
recall_data <- function(d, scoring = c("correct", "correct_strict")) {
  scoring <- match.arg(scoring)
  d$trials |>
    filter(task == "test", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    filter(!(condition == "pretest" & as.logical(guess_correct) %in% TRUE)) |>
    group_by(participant_id, cycle = as.integer(cycle), condition) |>
    summarise(value = mean(as.logical(.data[[scoring]])), n_items = n(), .groups = "drop")
}

# Mean, SD and n per cycle x condition, the shape used by the figures (and by `original_pred`).
cell_summary <- function(long) {
  long |>
    group_by(cycle, condition) |>
    summarise(mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), sd = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
              n = sum(!is.na(value)), .groups = "drop")
}

# Per-participant contrasts from long data (columns participant_id, cycle, condition, value).
wide_cells <- function(long) {
  long |> pivot_wider(id_cols = participant_id, names_from = c(condition, cycle), values_from = value)
}

# One-sample t-test on a contrast, reported as the equivalent 2 x 2 repeated-measures F.
# Takes either a vector of per-participant contrasts or list(N, mean, sd). NULL if N < 2.
contrast_test <- function(x) {
  if (is.numeric(x)) {
    x <- x[!is.na(x)]
    x <- list(N = length(x), mean = if (length(x)) mean(x) else NA, sd = if (length(x) > 1) sd(x) else NA)
  }
  if (x$N < 2 || is.na(x$sd) || x$sd == 0) return(NULL)
  df <- x$N - 1; se <- x$sd / sqrt(x$N); t <- x$mean / se
  tibble(N = x$N, estimate = x$mean, sd = x$sd,
         ci_low = x$mean - qt(0.975, df) * se, ci_high = x$mean + qt(0.975, df) * se,
         t = t, df = df, F = t^2, p = 2 * pt(-abs(t), df), pes = t^2 / (t^2 + df), dz = x$mean / x$sd)
}

# The key statistic: the cycle x condition interaction on predictions,
# (pretest - read in Cycle 2) - (pretest - read in Cycle 1).
key_contrast <- function(d) {
  w <- wide_cells(prediction_data(d))
  if (!all(c("read_1", "pretest_1", "read_2", "pretest_2") %in% names(w))) return(NULL)
  contrast_test((w$pretest_2 - w$read_2) - (w$pretest_1 - w$read_1))
}
original_key <- contrast_test(original_contrast)

# contrast_test() with extra label columns; NULL (dropped by bind_rows) when it cannot be computed.
labelled_test <- function(x, ...) {
  r <- contrast_test(x)
  if (is.null(r)) NULL else mutate(r, ...)
}

# Side-by-side figure: any number of studies, one panel each, same axes. Each argument is a
# cell summary (cycle, condition, mean, sd, n). Error bars are 95% CIs of the cell means.
comparison_plot <- function(..., ylab = "Predicted number correct (out of 16)", ylim = c(0, 16)) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    mutate(Study     = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           Cycle     = factor(paste("Cycle", cycle)),
           Condition = factor(condition, levels = c("read", "pretest"), labels = c("Read", "Pretest")),
           half      = ifelse(n > 1, qt(0.975, n - 1) * sd / sqrt(n), NA),
           label     = sprintf("n = %d", n))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.75)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = Cycle, y = mean, fill = Condition)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.7) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - half, ymax = mean + half), position = dodge, width = 0.2, na.rm = TRUE) +
    facet_wrap(~ Study, nrow = 1) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = ylim) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(Read = "grey60", Pretest = "#1E6E76")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = ylab, fill = NULL,
         caption = paste(sprintf("%s: n = %d", levels(df$Study), tapply(df$n, df$Study, max)), collapse = "   ")) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
pilot_b <- read_phase(experiment_id_pilot_b)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
have_pilot_b <- !is.null(pilot_b)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Interaction (prediction points)` = "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", F = "", p = "", `ηp²` = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Interaction (prediction points)` = sprintf("%.2f", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         F = sprintf("F(1, %d) = %.2f", r$df, r$F),
         p = format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
         `ηp²` = sprintf("%.2f", r$pes))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original (Exp 3)", original_key),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) key_contrast(phase1)),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) key_contrast(phase2))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrlllr",
               caption = "Key comparison: cycle × condition interaction on predictions, i.e. the change from Cycle 1 to Cycle 2 in (pretest − read) predicted recall, out of 16.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction
I'm very interested broadly in learning science and decision making in learning, and I dipped a little into reward prediction error and spaced learning studies last quarter which I really enjoyed. I thought it would be interesting to replicate a study that tried to manipulate other metacognitive variables, and the use of different pre-testing and reminder/feedback experiments like Pan & Rivers ran seemed like a good fit.

For the construction of the experiment, the procedure includes a test of participants pairing words - for the pairs themselves, I'll use the same data set of paired words taht Pan & Rivers pulled from, coming from Huelser & Metcalfe, 2012, and Nelson et al., 1998(norms). For bulding out the experiment itself, I'll send out some agents to build out the several parts of it, from my understanding of the method that Pan & Rivers designed. Since the materials & experiment sample is also public, I have a good insight into what exactly the structure of the site and bounds of the experiment is for a participant. 

The first part for the participant is the reading phase, where word pairs are randomly assigned for participants to be flashed pairs and attempt to internalize for the next session, which is the pre-test trial. Participants should likely fail most, and next they will predict their rate. After 5 minutes of a distractor activity(Tetris was used by Pan & Rivers - should be negligible & any non-semantic game should be viable but I can likely send an agent out to integrate or create a Tetris version for replicability's sake), they will enter the test phase. Unlike the 5-seconds for guessing and correct answer flashing on reading/pre-test trials, this test phase is self-paced, and following that, participants will have one more feedback display before finishing. This entire cycle is repeated once more with a new set of randomized pairs. A concern I might have lean more logistical, but the length of this test is around 30 minutes, so not sure how we are incentivizing participants. 

For the statistical test, we want to focus on how people's metacognitive recognition of pre-testing working better plays out - the idea the pre-testing is better has essentially came to consensus from previous research. We want to take into account people's predictions in both cycles, and like Pan & Rivers had shown, the reminders of their own predictions throughout both cycles, and better performance with pre-testing should make participants' predictions in Cycle 2 shift towards pretesting more. The key statistic that does this is a 2x2 ANOVA test across the gap in Cycle 1 between pre-test & read trials, gap in Cycle 2 in pre-test and read trials, and the change in that gap. The results from the original paper was most importantly, ηp² = .18, which essentially values how big the shift between C1 and C2 is on average, or the share of the variability in belief that's actually explained by the belief, along with p = .0017, and F = 10.92. 

An extension possibility I am considering is assigning a control group with no feedback displays. All participants got feedback in experiment 3, so the shift in predictions could also come from task reptition or Cycle 2 benefits. The original study compares Experiment 3 to Experiment 1, which runs on a different platfor, so a control group could test any causal link claims potentially? The key test is actually still identical if this is built out, it just requires a larger sample size.


## Methods

### Power analysis

:The key effect in the original experiment (for part 3 that I'm specifically replicating) is the practice condition, or how a word pair was studied with either pre-testing or pure reading, and which cycle round of the experiment the participant was in, and applying analysis to the participant's predictions for each. This results in a 2x2 ANOVA with two factors and two levels for each factor for cycle and testing condition, with key statistics of $F(1, 51) = 10.92$, $p = .0017$, $\eta_p^2 = .18$. The table shows that to detect the effect with .5, it would require n to be 40, 52, & 64 for 80%, 90%, & 95% power, respectively. For avoiding an underpowered study, budget constraints limit a full 2.5x sample size analysis, which would be 130 participants taking a ~35 minute test(with 10 minutes of tetris).

Since our budget constraints would be around ~70 participants for this study, power analysis at that sample size would vary in how much the original effect is shown. If the effect is equal to the original study's amount, a replication with n = 70(assuming a similar 13.6% exclusion rate as original experiment, so payment would be for n = 81) would yield 97% power, but only 47% if the effect size is half as such. Therefore, if the study is ran, it would only be able to detect the original effect size from it's original amount to about a 25% smaller effect(at 81% power), but would be fairly underpowered to meaningfully detect a smaller effect size. An option I can use to maximize budget and  use is Prolific's running slots for participants, adding participants that meet exclusion criteria until I have enough sampling to meet 70, as well as using confidence intervals along with p values in my analysis to help take this into account.

```{r}
#| label: power
# The key test is the 2 x 2 within-subjects interaction, which is a one-sample t-test on each
# participant's contrast (see Key statistics), so power is computed for that test from the
# original's standardized effect, d_z = mean / SD of the contrast.
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.t.test(delta = original_key$dz, sd = 1, power = pw, sig.level = 0.05,
                    type = "one.sample", alternative = "two.sided")$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_total = ceiling(n))
})

two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original_n)

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N analysed"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original interaction (d_z = %.2f; ηp² = %.2f, F(1, %d) = %.2f), two-sided alpha = .05.",
               original_key$dz, original_key$pes, original_key$df, original_key$F))
```


### Planned sample

I will recruit participants on Prolific until at least 70 individuals completed the study passing exclusion criteria. Eligibility requirements in selection match the original Experiment 3 as much as possible, meaning residents of North America, the UK, Austrialia, or New Zealand that are fluent in english with a ≥90% approval rating. 


### Materials

I will use the materials Pan & Rivers used, which were 64 cue and target word pairs from Huelser & Metcalfe (2012), who drew them from the Nelson et al. (1998) norms. Each word pair contained words of at least four letters with associative strengths of .5-.54, and backward associative strengths of 0, which I obtained from their OSF stimuli file.

The instructional screens were also followed closely as well as prediction screens from the original experiment (Experiment 1 is the only published live video, but it's word pairs are structured the same and the video is linked below)

https://osf.io/htjqz/files/24efh


### Procedure

The overall experiment takes around ~30 minutes for participants, starting off with informed consent and demographic questions(including age, gender, and english proficiency confirmation)

In the first cycle, 32 pairs are presented in random order, with half of them shown through reading and the other half through pretesting. Both reading and pretesting conditions here showed the words and option to type in a word for 5 seconds, with the full pair appearing after that time for the pretesting pairs. After this session, participants made two predictions in random order predicting from 0-16 how well they could do next test. They then play Tetris for 5 minutes as a distractor activity with no words, after which they undergo the recall test on the same 32 pairs all at once, with no feedback after each pair, and paced at their own level, allowing as much time as needed to complete the pair. After this, the cycle is complete and participants are shown their scores for each part of the cycle. This is where participants are required to answer a question that asks them to place whether their prediction was higher, lower than, or the same as their performance for each condition. This is helpful because it functions as an attention check, and also helps emphasize to participants their performance on read pairs and pretested pairs. After this, participants are shown are shown their performance feedback screen once more, and they continue to Cycle 2.

Cycle 2 is the same structure as Cycle 1, with 32 new pairs of words, and ending with feedback only of their scores, no reminders of predictions. They are then asked a question about where they attribute their performance, likely improved performance, to testing conditions, performance over time, and others.

### Analysis plan

The main analysis that will be used is the cycle and testing condition in a repeated measure ANOVA of the four differentiated predictions, where the prediction is that the amount of positive difference between pretesting over reading conditions will increase from Cycle 1 to Cycle 2. 

Participants will be excluded if they didn't complete the study, failed the Cycle 1 attention check, or missed any of the four predictions. For analysis that excludes specific pairs, Pan & Rivers, along with Huelser & Metcalfe excluded pretested pairs that were guessed correctly from scoring in recall portions. I have also made the main recall scoring lenient for case, typographical, and punctuation errors, but a strict raw scoring basis is also scored in case.

Analyses along with the paired 2x2 ANOVA would be t-tests within each of the cycles, the pretesting effect itself within recall, and an analysis for a subgroup of participants that showed the effect itself substantively on the Cycle 1 criteria test. I'll also compare my confidence intervals to zero and the original's estimate, and whether my 95% interval excludes or includes 1.4 points from the original experiment.


### Differences from the original study



| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | Used open-source collector (https://github.com/gikeymarcia/Collector) | jsPsych on Github Pages + Firebase | Unlikely, interface for participants is the same |
| Attribution options in final question | 5 categories | Reconstructed clearer wording of two main options | No, attribution input from participants is not used in analysis |
| Spelling/Grammar Leniency | Not specified | allows minute mistakes | Unlikely, leniency is not strict enough to where participants could cite words entirely different |

### Methods addendum (post data collection)

### Pilot B

Five participants completed Pilot B, where the median completion time was ~33 minutes, but there were structural issues in conduction of the study portions themselves that weren't apparent in Pilot A. 

Two participants each left three predictions unanswered, so there were six missing predictions across the study. The interface will be changed to require an input from participants as a result.

While four participants rated the instructions as "very clear", and one rated them as "clear", of the ten comparison & attention check questions across participants, four were answered correctly, four incorrectly, and two couldn't be scored because the predictions themselves were missing. As a result, only one of five participants fully completed all four predictions and passed all comparison checks. 

While comparison check questions followed Pan & Rivers original study, for participant understanding & ensuring focus on the true effect, prose for instructions/attention checks will be rewritten to be clearer for participants.

```{r}
#| label: pilot-b-preparation
#| include: false
#| eval: !expr have_pilot_b
pb_participants <- pilot_b$participants
pb_trials <- pilot_b$trials
pb_full <- pilot_b$complete |> arrange(pilot_label)
pb_full_trials <- pb_trials |> semi_join(pb_full, by = "participant_id")
pb_predictions <- pb_full_trials |> filter(task == "prediction")
pb_checks <- pb_full_trials |> filter(task == "attention_check")
pb_recall <- pb_full_trials |> filter(task == "test")
pb_guesses <- pb_full_trials |> filter(task == "pretest_guess")
pb_games <- pb_full_trials |> filter(task == "distractor")

# person_id is an anonymous grouping code used only to reconcile repeat page loads.
# Prolific IDs and their lookup file are not included in this public snapshot.
pb_consented_people <- pb_trials |>
  filter(task == "consent", as.logical(consented) %in% TRUE) |>
  distinct(participant_id) |>
  left_join(select(pb_participants, participant_id, person_id), by = "participant_id") |>
  distinct(person_id)
pb_completed_people <- pb_full |> distinct(person_id)

pb_session_summary <- pb_full |>
  select(participant_id, pilot_label, duration_minutes) |>
  left_join(pb_predictions |> group_by(participant_id) |>
              summarise(predictions_present = sum(!is.na(prediction)), .groups = "drop"),
            by = "participant_id") |>
  left_join(pb_checks |> group_by(participant_id) |>
              summarise(checks_correct = sum(as.logical(passed) %in% TRUE),
                        checks_incorrect = sum(as.logical(passed) %in% FALSE),
                        checks_unscorable = sum(is.na(passed)), .groups = "drop"),
            by = "participant_id") |>
  left_join(pb_recall |> group_by(participant_id) |>
              summarise(recall_trials = n(),
                        recall_blank = sum(is.na(answer) | trimws(answer) == ""),
                        recall_lenient = sum(as.logical(correct) %in% TRUE),
                        recall_strict = sum(as.logical(correct_strict) %in% TRUE), .groups = "drop"),
            by = "participant_id") |>
  left_join(pb_guesses |> group_by(participant_id) |>
              summarise(guess_blank = sum(as.logical(guess_empty) %in% TRUE), .groups = "drop"),
            by = "participant_id") |>
  mutate(analysis_eligible = participant_id %in% pilot_b$keep$participant_id)

pb_clarity <- pb_full_trials |>
  filter(task == "feedback_likert") |>
  mutate(clarity_index = map_dbl(response, ~ as.numeric(fromJSON(.x)$instructions_clear)))
```

#### Deviations from the preregistered plan

The initial sample size was planned to be 70 analyzable participants, however given budget constraints, having the same sample size as the original study seemed like a feasible alternative. Recruitment overall ended at 52 participants as well, as recruiting until 52 non-excluded participants would mean a much higher sample size that would be out of budget constraints, given the 57.7% pass rate of participants to be included in the analysis. 


## Results

### Data preparation

Participants and trial records used participant IDs as identifiers, and overall sessions were complete if it was counted as complete from beginning to end including consent & final debrief question on validity of instructions given. Participants entered the actual analysis if they answered the prediction & performance comparison questions of their own answers correctly for all four recall predictions. This is especially important because it not only functions as an attention check, but it is important for the participant to see their typically superior performance in the pre-test condition and understand that before predicting for Cycle 2. For each participant, the difference between predicted recall for pretested and read matching pairs were calculated for each cycle, and the Cycle 1 difference was subtracted from the Cycle 2 difference. For the actual recall, pretested pairs the participant guessed correctly were omitted from analysis and the proportion of pairs recalled in each cycle and practice condition were scored leniently and factored into prediction viewings for participants.

### Confirmatory analysis
The primary test to look at was the cycle & practice condition interaction in a 2x2 repeated ANOVA for the predicted recall. 

In Cycle 1, participants predicted recalling an average of 7.13 pretested pairs and 7.23 read pairs, so a pretest condition premium difference of -.1 pairs. In Cycle 2, participants predicted recalling 8.37 pretested pairs and 8.07 read pairs, a pretest premium of +0.3 pairs.

With an overall prediction increase of 0.4 across cycles, we have a 95% CI [−0.28, 1.08], F(1, 29) = 1.46, p = .236, and a partial η² of .048

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
preds <- prediction_data(phase1)
key1  <- key_contrast(phase1)

# 2 (cycle) x 2 (condition) repeated-measures ANOVA on predictions, as in the original.
# The cycle:condition row is the key test; it equals the contrast test reported below.
anova_ok <- n_distinct(preds$participant_id) >= 2
if (anova_ok) {
  fit <- tryCatch(
    aov(value ~ factor(cycle) * factor(condition) + Error(factor(participant_id) / (factor(cycle) * factor(condition))),
        data = preds),
    error = function(e) { message("ANOVA could not be fitted: ", conditionMessage(e)); NULL })
  if (!is.null(fit)) print(summary(fit))
} else {
  message("ANOVA not run: it needs at least two analysed participants; there are ",
          n_distinct(preds$participant_id), ".")
}

if (!is.null(key1)) {
  key1 |>
    transmute(N, `Interaction (points)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              F = sprintf("F(1, %d) = %.2f", df, F), p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
              `ηp²` = sprintf("%.2f", pes), `d_z` = sprintf("%.2f", dz)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Key test: cycle × condition interaction on predictions.")
} else {
  message("Key test not computed yet: needs at least two analysed participants whose contrasts are not all identical.")
}

# Follow-up tests reported in the original: pretest vs read predictions within each cycle.
w <- wide_cells(preds)
if (nrow(w) >= 2 && all(c("read_1", "pretest_1", "read_2", "pretest_2") %in% names(w))) {
  follow <- bind_rows(
    labelled_test(w$pretest_1 - w$read_1, Comparison = "Cycle 1: pretest − read"),
    labelled_test(w$pretest_2 - w$read_2, Comparison = "Cycle 2: pretest − read")
  )
  if (nrow(follow) > 0) follow |>
    transmute(Comparison, N, `Difference (points)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              t = sprintf("t(%d) = %.2f", df, t), p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Predictions for pretested minus read pairs within each cycle.")
}
```

### Replication assessment

In Pan & Rivers original experiment, the predicted pretesting pair premium shifted from -0.71 in Cycle 1 to +0.69 in Cycle 2, increasing by 1.4 pairs across Cycles, with a 95% CI [0.55, 2.26]. The replication still shows the same effect directionally, but a smaller size of +0.4 pairs. The confidence interval also included zero and ended at +1.08 pairs. The effect size is much smaller, partly due to budget constraints, with lower power to reveal effect sizes if the true effect is similar to the original experiment, along with a much higher failure rate for attention & confirmation checks for participants.



```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- original_key
rep  <- key1

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original (Exp 3)"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Interaction (points)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              `ηp²` = sprintf("%.2f", pes), `d_z` = sprintf("%.2f", dz),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: change from Cycle 1 to Cycle 2 in the pretest − read difference in predictions.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.2f points. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

```{r}
comparison_plot(`Original (Exp 3)` = original_pred,
                `Phase 1: replication` = cell_summary(prediction_data(phase1)))
```

### Exploratory analyses

The recall testing showed better performance for pretesting conditions as expected across Cycles, and participants recalled 17.5% more pretested than read trained pairs in Cycle 1, and 13.5% better in Cycle 2. In participants who showed an advantage for recall testing in pretested pairs in Cycle 1, those 22 participants had their predicted pretesting advantage increase by 0.36 pairs.


```{r}
#| label: exploratory
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory. (1) The pretesting effect on recall, which the predictions are supposed to track.
rec <- recall_data(phase1)
rw  <- wide_cells(rec)
if (nrow(rw) >= 2 && all(c("read_1", "pretest_1", "read_2", "pretest_2") %in% names(rw))) {
  rec_tests <- bind_rows(
    labelled_test(rw$pretest_1 - rw$read_1, Cycle = 1),
    labelled_test(rw$pretest_2 - rw$read_2, Cycle = 2)
  )
  if (nrow(rec_tests) > 0) rec_tests |>
    transmute(Cycle, N, `Pretest − read (proportion)` = sprintf("%.3f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              t = sprintf("t(%d) = %.2f", df, t), p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
              d = sprintf("%.2f", dz)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: criterial-test recall advantage for pretested pairs (original: t(51) = 6.67 and 5.99).")
}

# (2) The original's subgroup analysis: participants who showed a pretesting effect on recall in Cycle 1.
if (nrow(rw) >= 2) {
  sub_ids <- rw$participant_id[(rw$pretest_1 - rw$read_1) > 0]
  sub <- contrast_test({
    pw <- wide_cells(prediction_data(phase1)) |> filter(participant_id %in% sub_ids)
    (pw$pretest_2 - pw$read_2) - (pw$pretest_1 - pw$read_1)
  })
  if (!is.null(sub)) {
    sub |>
      transmute(N, `Interaction (points)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
                F = sprintf("F(1, %d) = %.2f", df, F), p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
                `ηp²` = sprintf("%.2f", pes)) |>
      knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: key interaction among participants with a Cycle 1 pretesting effect on recall (original: F(1, 38) = 18.23, ηp² = .32).")
  }
}

# (3) Pretest guesses and data quality.
trials |>
  filter(participant_id %in% keep$participant_id, task == "pretest_guess") |>
  group_by(Cycle = cycle) |>
  summarise(`Guessed correctly` = mean(as.logical(guess_correct)),
            `Left blank` = mean(as.logical(guess_empty)), .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3, caption = "Pretest guesses (original: .035 correct in Cycle 1, .053 in Cycle 2).")

trials |>
  filter(participant_id %in% keep$participant_id, task == "distractor") |>
  group_by(Cycle = cycle) |>
  summarise(`Mean Tetris lines` = mean(tetris_lines), `Mean keypresses` = mean(tetris_keypresses),
            `No keypresses` = sum(tetris_keypresses == 0), .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, caption = "Distractor task engagement.")

# (4) Exit questions and the Cycle 2 attribution question.
exit <- trials |>
  filter(task == "exit_questions", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  mutate(resp = map(response, ~ fromJSON(.x))) |>
  transmute(read_eff    = map_dbl(resp, ~ as.numeric(.x$read_effectiveness %||% NA)),
            pretest_eff = map_dbl(resp, ~ as.numeric(.x$pretest_effectiveness %||% NA)),
            preference  = map_chr(resp, ~ as.character(.x$preference %||% NA)))
if (nrow(exit) > 0) {
  exit |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Reading effectiveness (0-10)` = mean(read_eff, na.rm = TRUE),
              `Pretesting effectiveness (0-10)` = mean(pretest_eff, na.rm = TRUE),

}
trials |>
  filter(task == "attribution", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
```

## Discussion


### Summary of replication attempt

The replication displays the benefit of pretesting in recall testing, but was fairly inconclusive in revealing evidence that participants updated their predictions to reflect that benefit. The predictions still shifted in the same direction as the original study to prefer pretesting, but was much smaller. This smaller effect, as well as the restricted sample size, may also contribute to participants remembering more pretested pairs overall in both cycles, but the main effect of the shift across cycles as a relative point is also less apparent.

### Commentary

A challenge that may have contributed to the high failure rate, which could have tainted participant understanding is due to the Cycle 1 comparison questions and how participants interpreted them. In the questions given to participants after Cycle 1, their real scores as well as their predictions were shown to them in a table of four values. In the following page, they would have to confirm which scores were higher or lower than their predictions, which is intended to help participants fully understand the degree to which pre-testing is effective in their performance, as well as function as an attention check. An incorrect answer in these questions shows difficulty in seeing that pre-testing is functionally better than reading pairs to learn the pairs. We also cannot distinguish among these possibilities, but 22 of 52 participants were excluded as a result. In the original experiment, 8 of 62 participants were excluded for failed attention checks  by Pan and Rivers. Since this is such a drastic change, it's possible that the sample of 30 used disproportionately reflects participants who specifically remembered and answered correctly.


A follow up could keep each prediction and score visible during comparison questions, ensuring participants cross reference answers and do not let them pass until answering correctly.

# Phase 2: Extension

**Track:** Rescue

## Rationale

In Phase 1, participants increased their pretesting predictions .4 pairs on average, smaller than the original premium of 1.4, and the confidence interval of [-0.28, 1.08] included zero. Most importantly, 22 of 52 recruited participants failed the exclusion criteria, which could be due to a variety of procedural reasons, that display a large portion of participants not internalizing improved pretesting effects.

Since the comparison questions require comparison with participants own performance, not having the table of their four scores visible to cross reference when answering could be an issue. It could be a result of forgetting values for their scores or not paying attention to those values before advancing. In Phase 2, questions will have values of participants scores shown as they answer for each practice condition & prediction. This way, we can also restrict the question so participants must answer correctly before they continue, with another sepearate purely function attention check soon after, recognizing their score. I would expect both failure rates to decrease to around 13.3%, similar to the original experiment, as well as likely a larger effect size if more participants have identified the effect more clearly.


## Changes from Phase 1


| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sample | Recruitment ended at 52 participants with 30 analyzed | We can recruit a new sample with 30 participants, consistent with Phase 1 | Budget constraints reduce my sample size, or recruiting until 30 valid participants as a stopping point would be ideal |
| 2 | Checks | Predictions & scores are shown on one screen, and feedback questions about their performance are shown on the following screen to participants | Each comparison question displays the participant's own prediction & performance while the questions are asked | Participants can make the comparison without misremembering, and are also required to answer correctly and understand pre-testing's effect  |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

I will recruit 30 participants on Prolific, using the same eligibility criteria as in Phase 1, with the updated attention checks & feedback procedure. Recruitment will stop at 30 participants, and I will apply the same analysis to exclude if participants fail the purely functional attention checks. I expect the failure rate to decrease from 42.3%, but also expect increases in the original effect of the study. If we assume 4 participants fail attention checks, we see that the study has approximately  19% power to detect the effect size of Phase 1. With this low power, I would still at least expect the direction effect of improvement to be larger on average than Phase 1's results, as it would less so be participants who are already more inclined to be or were more aware of the pretesting effect.

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
phase2_recruited <- 30L
phase2_exclusion_rate <- 0.1333
phase2_n <- round(phase2_recruited * (1 - phase2_exclusion_rate))

p1_key <- if (have_data) key_contrast(phase1)
if (!is.null(p1_key)) {
  phase2_power <- power.t.test(
    n = phase2_n, delta = p1_key$dz, sd = 1, sig.level = .05,
    type = "one.sample", alternative = "two.sided", strict = TRUE
  )$power
  phase2_half_width <- qt(.975, phase2_n - 1) * p1_key$sd / sqrt(phase2_n)

  tibble(
    `Recruited N` = phase2_recruited,
    `Assumed exclusion rate` = scales::percent(phase2_exclusion_rate, accuracy = 0.01),
    `Projected analysed N` = phase2_n,
    `Phase 1 benchmark (d_z)` = round(p1_key$dz, 2),
    `Power against zero` = scales::percent(phase2_power, accuracy = 1),
    `Phase 1 CI half-width (items)` = round((p1_key$ci_high - p1_key$ci_low) / 2, 2),
    `Expected Phase 2 CI half-width (items)` = round(phase2_half_width, 2)
  ) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Phase 2 power and precision using the Phase 1 prediction interaction as the planning benchmark.")
} else {
  message("Phase 1 data are needed to calculate the Phase 2 power benchmark.")
}
```

## Analysis plan

I will use the same primary test as in Phase 1, and for each participant, I will subtract the Cycle 1 difference from Cycle 2. This mean will be used in the two sided ANOVA, for cycle and practice condition of pretesting or reading. The main analysis will use Phase 2 data only, and participants must complete the study's comparison questions even if they fail attention checks - I will compare these values of failure rates & wrong answers on these questions as well as failures of attention checks before comparing alongside ANOVA tests.

```{r}
              p2_key$estimate, p2_key$ci_low, p2_key$ci_high, p2_key$df, p2_key$F, p_text, p2_key$pes, p2_key$dz))
}
```
